profile.purpose: Explain why the US military's OG-107 reverse sateen fatigue pants used such an effective fabric. It walks through weave structures and the 1940s–50s MIT-led fabric research and field testing behind the fabric.
profile.thesis: The OG-107 fatigue's reverse sateen is a dense sateen weave flipped to be weft-faced, so the weft shields the structural warp yarns. Research and combat-course testing by Stanley Backer and Ernest Ralph Kaswell showed this made it far more durable in real forward-motion wear than herringbone twill or denim. It was also more comfortable and more wind- and water-resistant, and vintage pairs are inexpensive today.
key_takeaways: OG = olive green shade 107; 'fatigues' were named for the fatiguing work done in them, which drove their wide, untailored, movement-friendly design.
Exterior patch pockets use the same thick fabric and add durability, comfort and easy repair without compromising the pants if holed.

Weaves are distinguished by interlacement points: plain weave has the most (stiff, durable), twill fewer with diagonal offsets (flexible, but tears run down channels and the fabric skews), sateen the fewest with long floats.
Herringbone twill reverses the offset every few rows, stabilising the fabric and stopping tear propagation; it is cited as about 15% stronger than regular denim and was the WWII standard.
Sateen's few interlacings allow many more yarns to be packed in, making it denser, more wind- and water-resistant, smooth enough to take finishes, and durable.
Backer argued fabrics should be flipped so the weft faces out and protects the warp; Kaswell's Camp Lee combat-course tests confirmed it.

Reverse sateen was found about 80% more durable than herringbone twill and 110% more than denim with the same yarns, but only in the forward/backward abrasion of actual wear; tested in all directions the fabrics were roughly equal.
Military specs left room for variation, so not all OG-107s or sateens are identical. Vintage pairs can be found cheaply on eBay, and orSlow makes a well-known modern reproduction.
The creator credits these findings as the foundation of modern outdoor brands and recommends the Articles of Interest 'Gear' series.

outline.title: The legendary sateen
outline.summary: Introduces OG-107 reverse sateen fatigues and claims the fabric was the military's most comfortable, durable, wind- and water-resistant of its time, thanks to one trick: flipping it inside out.

outline.title: Engineering better combat gear
outline.summary: The US military enlisted MIT researchers Stanley Backer and Ernest Ralph Kaswell, who ran lab tests and a simulated combat course at Fort/Camp Lee, Virginia.

outline.title: Comparing military fabrics
outline.summary: Poses the question of whether sateen is really better than herringbone twill, its predecessor, followed by the channel greeting.

outline.title: Design of military fatigues
outline.summary: Explains the OG-107 name and how fatigue work shaped the design: wide legs, roomy crotch and hips, exterior patch pockets. Notes why simple military design is so widely copied.

outline.title: The science of textile weaves
outline.summary: Introduces plain, twill and satin weaves, warp and weft, and interlacement points (interrupted by the sponsor read). Plain weave is the maximally interlaced, stiff, durable option.

outline.title: Twill weave analysis
outline.summary: Uses 3x1 denim to explain twill floats and offsets, which give flexibility. Their downsides are tears running down diagonal channels and the fabric skewing.

outline.title: Herringbone twill overview
outline.summary: Explains broken and herringbone twill, which reverses the offset to stabilise the fabric and stop tears. This made HBT about 15% stronger than denim and the WWII standard.

outline.title: The sateen breakthrough
outline.summary: After a snack break, shows vintage OG-107s bought on eBay and orSlow reproductions. Explains sateen's long floats and staggered interlacings: drapey and flexible, snags more easily, but resists tear runs.

outline.title: Fabric density and testing
outline.summary: Sateen's open structure allows denser yarn packing for wind and water resistance and durability. Covers Backer's paper and Kaswell's combat-course testing, with a comedic soldier skit.

outline.title: The importance of reverse weave
outline.summary: Covers the test results and Backer's key idea: flipping a warp-faced fabric to weft-faced so the weft shields the structural warp. This, combined with sateen's density, is why it won.

outline.title: Conclusion and legacy
outline.summary: Gives the durability figures (80% over HBT, 110% over denim) and explains they hold only for forward-motion wear. Calls the findings the foundation of outdoor brands and recommends the Articles of Interest 'Gear' series.

corrections.note: After saying sateen has no channel for anything to snag on, he corrects himself: sateen does snag more easily than other weaves, but its offset interlacement points make it harder for a tear to run down a channel as on twill.
Qualifies that the idea to flip fabrics may not have originated with Backer, but Backer was the one testing it and recommending it.
